state.frozen_policy_content:
Gentle AI native bounded review policy.

Only candidate-caused BLOCKER or CRITICAL findings may require correction. Pre-existing and base-only findings are follow-ups. One correction is bounded by the frozen original scope. Gates are informational and unmanaged; ordinary repository policy decides delivery.

findings.claim: ParseProjectLock now refuses a lock whose entries share a skill id, but SerializeProjectLock gained no matching guard and a newly added test asserts that two entries with the same id serialize successfully. Any caller that builds such a ProjectLock therefore writes a lock file that ParseProjectLock can never read back, which is precisely the write/read asymmetry the sibling version guard was added to prevent (its own doc comment states a write must never silently produce a lock the parser rejects). No test proves the serialize->parse round trip holds for the inputs SerializeProjectLock accepts.

The newly introduced double-quote/backslash escaper for the stamped candidate value has no externally observable assertion. validateCandidateKey only refuses an indicator character in the first byte, so a key with an interior double quote or backslash passes validation and reaches the escaper, yet every added test supplies a plain slug key containing neither character. Removing both replacement calls would leave the suite green while emitting frontmatter that closes the double-quoted scalar early.

Two of the five refusal rules added to validateCandidateKey (leading/trailing space, and an embedded colon-space or space-hash sequence) are never reached by any added test. The test named for a colon-space key passes a key whose first byte is a colon, which the earlier leading-indicator branch refuses first, and every refusal assertion is a bare non-nil-error check that cannot distinguish which rule fired. Both branches could be deleted without any test failing, so their behavior on invalid input is unproved.

The empty-metadata-block fallback test asserts only the stamped author line's two-space indent, leaving the provenance and candidate lines' fallback indentation unproved for that path; the four-space test pins all three stamped lines, so the asymmetry is an avoidable coverage gap in the newly added indent-selection behavior.

evidence: Inspected the complete candidate as presented: the full patches for engine/skills/project_lock.go and engine/skills/project_lock_test.go, and the two added task lines in openspec/changes/procedural-memory-lifecycle/tasks.md.

Trailing-data refusal in ParseProjectLock is correct and proved: a second decode into a raw message is compared against end-of-file, so a second JSON value and trailing non-JSON bytes both refuse, and both cases have added tests (engine/skills/project_lock_test.go:166-178).

Version normalization in SerializeProjectLock is proved in both directions: zero normalizes to 1 and any other non-1 version refuses, each with an added test (engine/skills/project_lock_test.go:180-194).

Determinism of SerializeProjectLock is now pinned by exact bytes rather than a modulo-2 indent heuristic, and equal-id ordering stability is asserted in both input orders (engine/skills/project_lock_test.go:84-154).

Removal of the zero-length slice guard before the opening-fence check in engine/skills/project_lock.go:200 is safe: splitting a string on newline always yields at least one element, so the first-element index cannot panic.

The shared line-classification helper preserves the previous block-end and keep/drop semantics exactly (blank or indented lines belong to the block, any other line ends it), so the refactor in engine/skills/project_lock.go introduces no behavior change on that path.

Inline metadata refusal and indentation reuse are each covered by added fixtures (engine/skills/project_lock_test.go:532-597), and the constants are now pinned by direct-literal tests (engine/skills/project_lock_test.go:196-201).
The tasks.md change is documentation only: it records the correction commit and defers target-path validation to the later writer slice; it has no runtime behavior and no test obligation of its own.
